Following marathon budget disputes in Brussels, Danish ministers lobbied EU leaders to tie migration explicitly to violent crime and accelerate plans for third-country deportation centers outside the bloc.

The Poison:
Packaging offshore deportation hubs as orderly administration normalizes indefinite legal limbo, stripping people of due process while creating unaccountable detention camps abroad under European financing.

The Breakdown & Plane Error:
This is a classic WHAT vs WHO substitution. Leaders claim to solve the administrative problem of border stability (WHAT) by systematically dehumanizing and criminalizing displaced people seeking refuge (WHO).

Social Physics Analysis:
Danish leadership runs a Smart Selfish maneuver. Facing domestic political heat, officials manufacture a criminal emergency, project societal strain onto asylum seekers, and hoard power while blocking genuine systemic integration.

The Trajectory: The Path of Fall into Destruction.
When you map the gap between stated intentions and ground-level results, it plots a direct trajectory toward Greater Evil. Abandoning legal obligations transforms standard governance into systemic cruelty.

The Unavoidable Truth: Externalizing asylum processing into non-EU return hubs is a willful evasion of international human rights treaties.
The Unavoidable Lie: Preaching that linking migration to crime creates European stability.

Alethekanon:
Replacing judicial due process with offshore encampments does not secure borders. It merely launders domestic political cowardice into institutionalized abuse while degrading the rule of law across Europe.

Awwthekanon:
People fleeing war and poverty deserve safety, fair hearings, and human dignity. Reducing their lives to political bargaining chips and pushing them into remote third-country holding cells ignores our shared humanity.

Brothekanon:
Politicians spend fourteen hours fighting over budgets, get nowhere, and immediately start blaming migrants for everything. Setting up offshore holding camps in Africa isn't border policy, it's just passing the buck.

"When a stranger resides with you in your land, you shall not wrong him. Love him as yourself, for you were strangers in Egypt." Leviticus 19:33-34 FAIL
Outsourcing vulnerable refugees to offshore camps violates the fundamental moral duty to protect the stranger.

After 14 hours of talks dominated by splits on energy and the EU budget, leaders are turning to migration and aid for Kyiv.

AI generated Text-to-speech

EU leaders returned Friday for their second day of marathon talks, with a discussion on migration set to descend into a showdown over whether to push for tougher controls.

Before those talks, Denmark called for new, tougher language linking migration to crime.

Earlier, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy made a direct pitch for more help amid a crisis of faith among allies over Donald Trump’s latest steps favoring Russia.

Leaders are expected to turn to the question of how to protect the bloc from Russian hybrid attacks, maritime security and the Middle East.

On Thursday, a three-hour argument over taxing car emissions derailed Antonio Costa’s carefully laid plans to tackle the biggest challenges facing the bloc: fixing its economy and sorting out its spending priorities, drawing ire from some diplomats.

As leaders piled into their motorcades around midnight after 14 hours of talks, they seemed as far away as ever on negotiations over the bloc’s next long-term budget — with the next serious round of talks slipping to November.

Stated Claim / Post Context:
Can the EU survive with far-right leaders running major member states? The answer is worrying

As the EU enters an unprecedented electoral supercycle, the question is whether it can defend its integrity as the forces challenging it gain influence over its institutions.

Actual Article Body:
EUobserver

Opinion

Europe is heading into an electoral moment without recent precedent. Four of its five most populous member states, Spain, France, Italy and Poland, are due to vote within the next 12 months – starting with Spain on 29 November.

If voters move further right, the combined effect could reshape the Union far more profoundly than any single national election.

Two shifts stand out. First, the firewall between the centre-right European People’s Party (EPP) and the hard-right is crumbling, even in Germany, its last bastion.

Hard-right parties sit in the governments of Italy, Czech Republic, Finland, Slovakia and Croatia, while Slovenia’s government relies on outside support from one.

Second, competition from the far-right is pushing established radical-right parties to harden their positions.

In Catalonia, Aliança Catalana is challenging Vox; in France, Éric Zemmour’s Reconquête, despite scoring single digits, is pressing on Marine Le Pen’s National Rally; in Italy, Roberto Vannacci’s National Future is challenging Giorgia Meloni’s Brothers of Italy; and in Poland, Grzegorz Braun’s Confederation of the Polish Crown is cannibalising the Confederation.

Under pressure, established conservatives tend to move towards these parties rather than hold the line, as Spain’s Partido Popular and France’s Les Républicains illustrate. Positions once on the margins become mainstream.

The implications go beyond immigration.

Le Pen and Vox leader Santiago Abascal advocate “national priority” in access to welfare and public services. Under pressure from the League and National Future, Meloni’s government has introduced a 30-percent cap on first-year classrooms for pupils without Italian citizenship, based on their birthplace or prior schooling.

Read more

A leaked AfD strategy paper reportedly goes further, proposing that national constitutions override EU law and reducing the Court of Justice to a forum for disputes between governments.

Stated Claim / Post Context:
Collins Pushes Back as Jackson Says He’s Open to Expanding Supreme Court

Sen. Susan Collins (R-ME) rejected expanding the Supreme Court during Thursday’s Senate debate after Democrat Troy Jackson said he was open to adding justices because the court “obviously is not working.”
The post Collins Pushes Back as Jackson Says He’s Open to Expanding Supreme Court appeared first on Breitbart.

Actual Article Body:
Sen. Susan Collins (R-ME) rejected expanding the Supreme Court during Thursday’s Senate debate after Democrat Troy Jackson said he was open to adding justices because the court “obviously is not working.”

Jackson backed term limits and stricter ethics rules while accusing members of the court of accepting gifts and travel from people with business before them:

I understand why we had Supreme Court that was supposed to be lifetime positions, but look, what we have now is something unbelievable. I mean, people that don’t have any ethics. People that are taking trips, people are taking you know gifts from people that are going to come before them. I mean, this is not I don’t think what our founding fathers expected whenever they set up you know this system. And so yeah, I think first and foremost we have to have real ethics reform that’s accountable that you can hold people do. I think that we should have term limits, and I’m not against putting more people on the court because this court obviously is not working. It’s working at the pass of the Donald Trump and the billionaire class. I mean, that’s who’s actually funding people like Thomas and Alito.

Collins responded that the court’s independence should take priority. She also rejected adding seats as a way to reshape the court. She said:

What we want is a Supreme Court that is insulated from politics. That was the whole idea of the judicial system, one of the three branches of government, parts of the checks and balances that the founders of this country envisioned. To try to pack the court by increasing the numbers goes completely against the vision of those who wrote the Constitution. I would also point out that I am the only Republican senator who voted for Justice Sotomayor, Justice Jackson, and Justice Kagan. Those three liberal women justices who were appointed by Democratic presidents, and that’s what I think the founders want. They don’t want the Supreme Court to be like Congress.

The Constitution leaves the number of Supreme Court seats unspecified. Congress established a six-member court in 1789, and its size changed several times before lawmakers set its membership at nine in 1869.
